html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Risk (PMBOK 8): an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more portfolio, program or project objectives.

Term Meaning
Threat A risk with a negative effect on objectives (delay, cost overrun, reputation damage)
Opportunity A risk with a positive effect (market share, cost savings, positive environmental impact)
Risk statement Written as cause → event → consequence so the risk is distinguished from its cause and effect
Issue A current condition or situation that may affect objectives. It has already occurred (or is occurring); a risk is a potential future event. An issue can arise from a poorly managed risk.
Individual vs overall risk Overall risk is the effect of uncertainty on the project as a whole (including individual risks). Responses use the same strategies but are applied to the whole project. If overall risk is too high the organization may cancel the project.
Risk appetite The degree of uncertainty an organization or individual will accept in anticipation of a reward; often quantified through a threshold
Risk threshold Measure of acceptable variation around an objective that reflects the appetite (e.g., ±5% on cost = lower appetite than ±10%)
Risk exposure Aggregate measure of the potential impact of all risks at a point in time
Risk response A planned or implemented action to address specific threats and opportunities
Ambiguity / uncertainty Ambiguity = unclear what to expect or which option is best. Uncertainty = lack of understanding or awareness. Neither always becomes a risk; collaborative problem-solving and more information often resolves them.
Project resilience Ability to absorb impacts and recover quickly from setbacks (high-impact, low-probability "black swan" events and emergent risks)

Goal of the domain: increase the probability and impact of positive risks and decrease the probability and impact of negative risks, building resilience and reducing uncertainty.

Exam angle

known-knowns are not risks (they are facts and requirements managed in scope). Identify risks means separating real risks from concerns, issues and assumptions.

2The Six Risk Processes

Process Focus area Purpose Key outputs Decision tools
Plan Risk Management Starts at conception; Planning Define how risk activities are conducted; finish early in the project Risk management plan Expert judgment, interviews, stakeholder analysis, meetings
Identify Risks Planning (iterative) Identify threats and opportunities; separate real risks from concerns Risk register, risk report; assumption/issue/lessons-learned updates Brainstorming, checklists, interviews, root cause analysis, assumption and constraint analysis, SWOT, document analysis, facilitation, prompt lists, AI
Perform Risk Analysis Planning (iterative) Qualitative analysis of probability and impact; quantitative analysis when needed Updated risk register and risk report Risk categorization, probability and impact assessment and matrix, simulation, sensitivity analysis, decision tree analysis, influence diagrams
Plan Risk Responses Planning Develop options, select strategies, agree actions for overall and individual risks; allocate resources and reserves Change requests; plan and baseline updates; register and report updated Strategies for threats / opportunities / overall risk, contingent strategies, alternative analysis, cost-benefit analysis, multicriteria decision analysis
Implement Risk Responses Executing Carry out the agreed responses Change requests; register, report, issue log, team assignments updated Influencing, PMIS, interpersonal skills
Monitor Risks Monitoring & Controlling Track identified risks, implementation of responses, new risks, effectiveness; assign risk owners Work performance information; change requests; plan and OPA updates; register and report Technical performance analysis, reserve analysis, audits, meetings

3Plan Risk Management

Begin when the project is conceived; complete early. The output is the risk management plan (part of the project management plan):

Element What it defines
Risk strategy General approach to managing risk
Methodology Approaches, tools and data sources
Roles and responsibilities Lead, support and team members for each risk activity
Funding Money for risk activities; protocols for using contingency and management reserves
Timing When and how often risk processes run; activities included in the schedule
Risk categories Ways to group risks; commonly a risk breakdown structure (RBS)
Stakeholder risk appetite Recorded as measurable thresholds around each objective; sets the acceptable overall exposure and informs the probability/impact scales
Probability and impact definitions Project-specific scales (typically five levels for a detailed approach, three for a simple one); the same scales evaluate threats (negative) and opportunities (positive)

Example of definitions (PMBOK 8 Table 4-2 style; each project sets its own):

Scale Probability Time impact Cost impact
Very high >70% >6 months >US$5M
High 51–70% 3–6 months US$1M–5M
Medium 31–50% 1–3 months US$501K–1M
Low 11–30% 1–4 weeks US$100K–500K
Very low 1–10% 1 week <US$100K

RBS example (PMBOK 8 Figure 4-5): Level 0 "all sources of project risk" → Level 1 Technical, Management, Commercial, External → Level 2 e.g., scope definition, requirements, technology (technical); project/portfolio management, resourcing, communication (management); contract terms, suppliers, client stability (commercial); legislation, exchange rates, environment/weather, competition, regulatory (external). The lowest RBS level doubles as a prompt list.

Not everything fits the scales: ethical risks, reputation and morale risks need judgment alongside the numbers.

4Identify Risks

  • Iterative: not all risks can be found at the start; new information means new identification (start of each phase or iteration).
  • Separate real risks from non-risks (concerns, issues, assumptions).
  • Include threats and opportunities.
Technique Use
Brainstorming, interviews, facilitation Gather ideas and expert views
Checklists Reuse lessons from similar projects; never exhaustive; also "definition of ready" checklists
Prompt lists Frameworks to trigger ideas: PESTLE (political, economic, sociocultural, technological, legal, environmental), TECOP (technical, environmental, commercial, operational, political), VUCA (volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity)
SWOT Adds internally generated risks
Assumption and constraint analysis Tests validity of assumptions and constraints; constraints can create opportunities when relaxed
Root cause analysis Finds underlying causes; supports categorization
Document analysis Plans, baselines, requirements, agreements, logs
AI / GenAI and data analytics Broaden identification and analysis (apply security and ethics checks)

Risk register (created here, updated by every later process):

Always at identification Optional extra data
Unique ID and description (cause-event-effect) Short title; risk category; current status
Potential risk owner Causes and effects on objectives
Potential responses Risk triggers (events/conditions showing a risk is about to occur)
WBS reference of affected activities; timing (identified, may occur, no longer relevant, action deadline)

Risk report: sources of overall project risk (key drivers) plus summary information on individual risks (number of threats and opportunities, distribution by category, metrics and trends); grows as later processes complete. Used to communicate the status of risk impact to stakeholders.

5Perform Risk Analysis

5.1 Qualitative analysis (done throughout the project)

Evaluate each individual risk for probability and impact using the plan's definitions; also consider degree of impact, manageability, timing, relationships with other risks and common causes.

  • Score = probability × impact; thresholds for high/medium/low come from OPAs or the risk plan.
  • Threats and opportunities share one matrix (negative impact definitions for threats, positive for opportunities).
  • Perceived differences between stakeholders are expected; explore them and record the assumptions behind each rating.
  • Low-scoring risks go on a watch list (kept in the register for future monitoring).
  • Risk categorization (by RBS source, by WBS area, by phase, by common root cause) shows where exposure is concentrated and supports generic responses to groups of risks.

5.2 Quantitative analysis (only when the project needs it)

Numerically analyzes the combined effect of individual risks and other uncertainty on overall objectives.

Technique What it tells you
Simulation (Monte Carlo) Models combined effects; produces e.g., the probability of finishing by a target date (S-curve). PMBOK 8 example: 10% chance of finishing by 13 May, 90% by 28 May
Sensitivity analysis Which risks or uncertainties have the most potential impact; displayed as a tornado diagram (ordered by strength of correlation)
Decision tree analysis Evaluates chains of decisions under uncertainty by calculating the expected monetary value (EMV) of each branch to pick the best path
Influence diagrams Show causal influences, time order and relationships; evaluated by simulation

EMV rule: EMV = probability × impact value (threats negative, opportunities positive). For a decision: add the EMVs along each branch (including any cost of the response) and choose the better (higher) EMV. A response that costs more than the EMV of the risk it addresses is usually not worth buying.

6Plan Risk Responses

Develop options, choose strategies, agree actions, assign owners, allocate resources and reserves, and insert response activities into the plans. Responses must be timely, cost-effective, realistic and agreed by the parties involved.

Key rules

  • Escalate when the risk is outside the project's scope or beyond the PM's authority. It is managed at program/portfolio/organization level; the receiving party must accept ownership; the project team does not monitor it further (it may stay in the register for information).
  • Avoid reduces probability to zero (or isolates objectives); mitigate reduces probability and/or impact. Early action is usually more effective than repairing damage later.
  • Transfer shifts impact and ownership of the response (insurance, performance bonds, warranties, guarantees, agreements); usually costs a risk premium. It does not make the risk disappear.
  • Exploit = make it certain (probability 100%); enhance = raise probability/impact; share = give ownership to the party best able to capture it.
  • Accept is active (set up a contingency reserve of time, money or resources) or passive (periodic review only). Suitable for low-priority risks or where other responses are not cost-effective.
  • Overall project risk uses the same ideas: avoid (extreme case: cancel the project; or remove high-risk scope), exploit (add high-benefit scope or adjust thresholds), transfer/share (joint venture, subcontracting, shared business structure), mitigate/enhance (replan, change scope or priority, reallocate resources), accept (overall contingency reserve).
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8 — terms the exam still uses]:
    • Residual risk: what remains after a response is implemented; keep reporting it.
    • Secondary risk: a new risk created by a response.
    • Fallback plan: used if the primary response proves ineffective.
    • Workaround: an unplanned response to a threat that has occurred, used when no response was planned or the planned one was not effective.
    • Contingent response: a response that runs only if a defined trigger happens. (PMBOK 8's "contingent response strategies" entry simply repeats the five opportunity strategies.)

Outputs: change requests (responses often need them), updates to the plans and baselines (schedule, cost, quality, resource, procurement), assumption log, risk register and risk report.

7Reserves (ECO: quantify risk and contingency financial allocations; manage financial reserves)

Contingency reserve Management reserve
Covers Known risks with active response strategies (known-unknowns) Unforeseen work within scope (unknown-unknowns), not specific identified risks
Where Time or money in the schedule or cost baseline; usually in the initial budget (PMBOK 8 allows it outside the baseline when managed explicitly) In addition to the baseline; never part of the cost baseline
Who releases Per the reserve protocols in the risk management plan (funding element) Typically senior management; in some organizations the PM or project team
Sized by Percentage, fixed amount or quantitative analysis; can be set at activity or project level; reduced as risks pass Management decision
  • Reserve analysis compares the remaining risk with remaining schedule and budget reserve to decide whether the reserve is sufficient; it also supports resilience.
  • Beyond PMBOK 8exam practice A reserve burning down faster than progress is a governance signal: reassess adequacy against remaining risks and inform the sponsor and governance bodies. Do not quietly top it up from management reserve.

8Implement Risk Responses

  • Risk owners carry out the agreed responses as planned; the PM influences and supports them.
  • Tools: influencing, PMIS, interpersonal skills.
  • Outputs: change requests, updates to the risk register, risk report, issue log, lessons learned register and team assignments.
  • If a response does not work: use the fallback plan or re-plan; new (secondary) risks go into the register.

9Monitor Risks

Tracks identified risks, response implementation, new risks and the effectiveness of responses, and keeps every risk owned.

Activity Notes
Risk reviews (reassessments) Status of existing risks and identification of new ones; regular cadence set in the plan (a register last updated at kickoff is a red flag)
Risk audit Examines the effectiveness of the risk management process (not individual risks); frequency defined in the risk management plan
Reserve analysis Is the reserve still enough for the remaining risk?
Technical performance analysis Compares technical achievement with plan (weight, defects, capacity); deviation can signal threats or opportunities
Risk becomes an issue Once it has occurred it is an issue: record it in the issue log, implement the planned response, update the register, inform stakeholders (Topic 30)
Closing risks Risks that can no longer occur are closed or archived; lessons learned captured
Communicate status Risk report, dashboards and meetings tell stakeholders how risk affects scope, schedule, cost and value

10ECO Examples: Security, Sustainability and AI Risks

  • Security (ECO example: poor IT security): keep it in the register with an owner and a response that reduces exposure (patching, controls, replacing the weak component). Insurance transfers financial loss but does not protect the data. The PM must work with IT/security to safeguard project information (Standard §2.5.1.3).
  • Sustainability risks (PMBOK 8 Standard §3.7): arise when activities fail to balance societal, economic and environmental considerations, e.g., prioritizing cost over environmental stewardship, ignoring community impact, underestimating sustainability-related regulatory compliance. Sustainability thinking helps the risk domain by enabling early identification and mitigation of long-term environmental, regulatory and societal risks and creates opportunities for innovation. Include them in the register and responses.
  • AI risks (PMBOK 8 Appendix X3): AI use carries ethical risks, chiefly bias, privacy and accountability. A human stays accountable for each decision and reviews AI output; apply security and ethics measures (Topic 08). AI can also assist risk work, e.g., drafting a risk register, which the PM must review for accuracy and completeness.
  • Compliance threats are treated as risks until they occur (Topic 23).

11Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Planning Formal risk management plan, RBS, scales set up front Lightweight; shared team understanding of risk appetite Formal plan for fixed/regulated parts, light for the rest
Identification Workshops at planning and phase gates; periodic reviews At the start of each sprint/iteration; continuous by the whole team Both, aligned to cadence
Visibility Risk register and risk report; steering committee Risks in the backlog (risk-adjusted backlog); information radiators; discussed in planning, reviews, retrospectives Register for fixed elements, backlog for iterative ones
Reserves and reviews Contingency and management reserves; risk reviews at milestones Short feedback loops reduce risk; risk review with stakeholders at the end of each iteration; adjust strategies Mix
Quantitative analysis Common on large or schedule-critical work Rare; frequent delivery reduces uncertainty Where needed
Beyond PMBOK 8 Timeboxed spikes to investigate risky unknowns

12Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

Tailoring considerations (PMBOK 8 §2.7.3): project size and complexity; organizational risk appetite and thresholds (and historical risk aversion); a holistic view across scope, schedule, cost and stakeholders; strategic importance of the project; development approach; flexibility in planning and implementing responses; complementary techniques (GenAI, data analytics); resilience planning (scenario planning, alignment with the organization's business continuity or emergency response plan).

PMBOK 8 examples: (1) solar power plant: regular meetings with key stakeholders, regular risk assessments, dedicated risk managers using simulation; (2) agile software project: risk assessment at the start of each sprint, risk review with stakeholders at the end of each iteration, risk-adjusted backlogs.

Interactions: stakeholders are key sources of risk information; scope, schedule and finance are directly affected (schedule reserves in predictive projects, replanning in adaptive ones; cost or revenue impact); risk responses often need change requests.

Outcome Check
Awareness of the environment (technical, social, political, market, economic) Environmental considerations are part of uncertainty and response evaluation
Proactive response to uncertainty Responses fit budget, schedule and performance constraints; a well-understood process exists
Minimal negative impact from unknowns Reserves in place and used, dates met, budget within variance threshold
Opportunities realized Mechanisms exist to identify, leverage and track them
Contingency used effectively Threats prevented proactively, limiting use of contingency
Resilience built Team knows the continuity or emergency plan; management reserve for unknown risks; structure and processes adapt quickly in a crisis

13Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. A risk that has occurred is an issue. Log it, execute the planned response, update the register. Do not just raise its probability to 100%.
  2. Every risk needs an active owner. If the owner leaves, assign a new one and confirm the response is ready. Re-scoring does not fill the gap.
  3. Use the project's own scales and thresholds (from the risk management plan); do not invent ratings.
  4. Positive risks deserve active responses (exploit, enhance, share), not a shrug.
  5. Contingency vs management reserve: known risks vs unknown-unknowns; the management reserve is outside the baseline and is not the PM's to spend unilaterally.
  6. Proportionality: compare response cost with the EMV of the risk. Do not pay $50K to remove a $30K exposure; do not accept a clear, cheap fix.
  7. Transfer is not elimination. Insurance or a contract moves the financial impact; the risk (and, for security or safety, the harm) may remain.
  8. Escalate only what is beyond scope or authority. After a valid escalation, ownership moves and the project stops monitoring it.
  9. Qualitative first; quantitative only when needed (e.g., the sponsor asks for the probability of hitting a date → simulation).
  10. Risk management is continuous. A register last updated at kickoff, or reviewed only at gates in an agile project, is the wrong answer.
  11. Reporting a response is not closing a risk. Report effectiveness and residual risk.
  12. First action when unsure: check the risk register and risk management plan, then act within them; use change control when a response changes the baseline.
  13. Agile: make risks visible in the backlog and discuss them in events; do not hide them in private reports or a monthly side meeting.
  14. Do not confuse risk with issue, assumption, constraint or concern.

14Exam Q&A

14.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A risk register entry reads "late deliveries". Which rewrite makes it a proper risk statement?

  • ABecause of its flood-zone plant, the supplier could halt supply and delay integration
  • BSupplier delays, which will probably cost the project a great deal of money later on
  • CIntegration has been delayed by six weeks because the supplies have already stopped
  • DThe supplier's only plant is located in a flood zone, which is a serious weakness
Show the answer

Answer: A. A risk statement links cause, event and consequence, so it differs from the cause alone, a vague effect or something that has already happened. The flood-zone location is only a cause, and the stopped supplies are not an uncertain event.

S2A team lists as a risk that the product must support 5,000 simultaneous users, which is a signed requirement in the backlog. How should the project manager treat it?

  • AAs a requirement to manage in scope, because a known fact is not a risk
  • BAs an assumption to be validated with the customer at the end of the project
  • CAs an opportunity to show off the capabilities of the chosen platform
  • DAs a high risk, because large requirements usually create technical difficulty
Show the answer

Answer: A. Known facts and requirements are managed in scope, not in the risk register, which holds uncertain events. Rating it as a risk, an assumption or an opportunity confuses the categories; any real uncertainty about meeting it would be a separate risk.

S3A change in the organization's data-center policy threatens several projects, and the project manager cannot influence the policy. What is the best response?

  • AAccept the risk and add a contingency reserve to the project budget
  • BKeep it in the project register and monitor it every week with the team
  • CMitigate it by lobbying the data-center committee to change the policy
  • DEscalate to the program or portfolio level and confirm that an owner accepts it
Show the answer

Answer: D. A risk outside the project's scope or beyond the manager's authority is escalated to the level that can manage it, and the receiving party must accept ownership. Accepting, lobbying or weekly monitoring keeps an unmanageable risk with the project.

S4The project manager buys a performance bond against a subcontractor's default, and the sponsor concludes that the delay risk has gone. What is the correct view?

  • AThe risk is avoided since the subcontractor can no longer default on the contract
  • BThe bond transfers the financial impact, but the delay risk remains
  • CThe risk is eliminated because the bond guarantees the work will be completed
  • DThe risk is mitigated to zero because the bond lowers its probability
Show the answer

Answer: B. Transfer shifts the financial impact and ownership of the response, usually for a premium, but it does not make the risk disappear, so schedule effects must still be watched. The other options treat a bond as eliminating, avoiding or removing the probability.

S5A university lab offers to co-develop a sensor that could cut unit costs by 30%, but the project lacks the expertise to capture the benefit alone. Which strategy fits?

  • AExploit, by using only internal staff to guarantee that the benefit is captured
  • BTransfer, by paying the lab to take over the project's risks
  • CShare, giving the lab part of the ownership so the benefit is captured
  • DAccept, by taking the benefit passively if it happens to occur
Show the answer

Answer: C. Sharing an opportunity gives ownership to the party best able to capture it, here the lab with the expertise. Exploiting needs a capability the project lacks, accepting is passive, and transfer is a strategy for threats.

S6To reduce the risk of delayed delivery, the team switches to air freight, which creates a new risk of customs hold-ups. How is the new risk described?

  • AA residual risk, which is simply what remains after the original response
  • BAn issue, because the customs hold-up has already begun to affect the schedule
  • CA workaround, since it is an unplanned response to the original risk
  • DA secondary risk, to go into the register with an owner and a response
Show the answer

Answer: D. A risk created by a response is a secondary risk and is recorded and managed like any other. Residual risk is what remains of the original risk, a workaround is a response to a risk that has occurred, and no customs hold-up has happened yet.

S7The sponsor asks for the probability of finishing by 30 June, taking all schedule risks into account together. Which analysis provides this?

  • AA tornado diagram, which ranks the risks by their potential impact
  • BA decision tree, which compares the expected value of alternative choices
  • CMonte Carlo simulation, giving a cumulative probability curve for the finish
  • DA probability and impact matrix, which scores each risk separately from the others
Show the answer

Answer: C. Quantitative analysis by simulation models the combined effect of individual risks and uncertainty and yields the probability of meeting a target date. The matrix scores risks one by one, a tornado diagram ranks sensitivity and a decision tree compares decision options.

S8The team wants to know which uncertainties could have the largest effect on the project's cost objective, ranked from strongest to weakest. Which display fits?

  • AA fishbone diagram of the causes behind earlier cost overruns
  • BA tornado diagram produced by sensitivity analysis of the cost model
  • CAn S-curve of the planned spending over the project's life
  • DA burnup chart showing the cost completed against the total scope
Show the answer

Answer: B. Sensitivity analysis shows which uncertainties carry the most potential impact and is displayed as a tornado diagram ordered by strength. The other displays show progress, causes or planned spend, not ranked sensitivity.

S9The sponsor of an agile program wants to know whether the program's risk management process is working, not the status of individual risks. Which activity answers this?

  • AA reserve analysis, which compares remaining reserves with remaining risk
  • BA risk audit, which examines the effectiveness of the risk management process
  • CA risk review, which reassesses the status of each of the existing risks
  • DA technical performance analysis, which compares achievement with the plan
Show the answer

Answer: B. A risk audit examines the effectiveness of the risk management process itself, whereas reviews reassess individual risks, reserve analysis tests sufficiency and technical performance analysis compares technical achievement with the plan.

S10During sprint planning, the team finds that the next story depends on an unfamiliar third-party API whose behavior nobody understands. What is the most suitable response?

  • ARun a timeboxed spike to learn about the API before committing the story
  • BCommit the story and hope that the API behaves as the vendor's brochure says
  • CRemove the story from the backlog permanently as too risky to attempt
  • DAsk the sponsor to approve a contingency reserve for any problems with the API
Show the answer

Answer: A. A timeboxed spike investigates a risky unknown cheaply before the team commits, which fits agile risk handling at the start of each iteration. Hoping, deleting the story or requesting reserve for an unexamined unknown does not reduce the uncertainty.

S11Building a feature in-house costs 80,000 with a 25% chance of 60,000 of rework. Buying a ready product costs 105,000 with a 5% chance of 20,000 of adaptation. Which has the better expected cost?

  • ANeither, because the options cannot be compared without a simulation
  • BBuy, with an expected cost of 105,000 against 140,000 for building
  • CBuy, because its probability of extra cost is only 5%
  • DBuild, with an expected cost of 95,000 against 106,000 for buying
Show the answer

Answer: D. Expected cost is the base cost plus probability times impact: building gives 80,000 plus 15,000, or 95,000, and buying gives 105,000 plus 1,000, or 106,000, so building has the better expected cost. A low probability alone, a miscalculated total or a demand for simulation does not change the comparison.

S12A hybrid project's register lists "supplier delivers late" with the trigger "supplier misses its first factory milestone". The supplier has just missed that milestone, but nothing has been delayed yet. What should the project manager do?

  • ARaise the risk probability to 100% in the register and take no further action
  • BClose the risk, because the trigger has already been recorded
  • CActivate the contingent response and update the register and stakeholders
  • DWait until the delivery date passes and then log the delay as an issue
Show the answer

Answer: C. A risk trigger shows that a risk is about to occur, so the contingent response is activated and the register and stakeholders are updated before any real delay turns it into an issue. Waiting, only rescoring or closing it wastes the early warning.

14.2 Recall Q&As

R1Define risk and name its two types.

Show the answer

An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on objectives. Threats are negative; opportunities are positive.

R2How does an issue differ from a risk?

Show the answer

An issue has already occurred or is occurring; a risk is a potential future event.

R3Name the five threat response strategies.

Show the answer

Escalate, avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept.

R4Name the five opportunity response strategies.

Show the answer

Escalate, exploit, share, enhance, accept.

R5Active vs passive acceptance?

Show the answer

Active: establish a contingency reserve (time, money, resources). Passive: no proactive action beyond periodic review.

R6Contingency reserve vs management reserve?

Show the answer

Contingency covers identified (known) risks with active responses; management reserve is held outside the baseline for unforeseen in-scope work (unknown-unknowns), released by management.

R7Risk appetite vs risk threshold?

Show the answer

Appetite is the degree of uncertainty accepted in anticipation of reward; threshold is the measurable acceptable variation around an objective that reflects that appetite.

R8What are the four known/unknown classifications?

Show the answer

Known-known (facts, not a risk), known-unknown (classic risk), unknown-known (hidden fact), unknown-unknown (emergent risk).

R9What does the risk management plan contain?

Show the answer

Risk strategy, methodology, roles and responsibilities, funding, timing, risk categories (e.g., RBS), stakeholder risk appetite, probability and impact definitions.

R10What does the risk register hold at identification?

Show the answer

Unique ID and description, potential risk owners and potential responses; optionally title, category, status, causes, effects, triggers, WBS reference and timing.

R11What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative analysis?

Show the answer

Qualitative ranks individual risks by probability and impact; quantitative numerically assesses the combined effect on objectives (simulation, sensitivity, decision trees, influence diagrams) and is used when needed.

R12What does a risk audit examine?

Show the answer

The effectiveness of the risk management process, at the frequency set in the risk management plan.

R13What happens to an escalated risk?

Show the answer

It is owned and managed at program, portfolio or organization level; the project team does not monitor it further (it may be recorded for information).

15Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Risk Uncertain event with positive or negative effect on objectives; cause-event-consequence
Risk vs issue Future potential vs already happened
Six processes Plan RM → Identify → Analyze → Plan Responses → Implement → Monitor
Risk management plan Strategy, methodology, roles, funding, timing, categories (RBS), appetite/thresholds, P&I definitions
Register vs report Register = individual risks; report = overall-risk sources + summary of individual risks
Qualitative Probability × impact; matrix; watch list; categorization
Quantitative Simulation (Monte Carlo), sensitivity (tornado), decision tree (EMV), influence diagrams
EMV Probability × impact; choose the better expected value; response cost vs EMV
Threat strategies Escalate, Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept
Opportunity strategies Escalate, Exploit, Share, Enhance, Accept
Acceptance Active = contingency reserve; passive = periodic review
Reserves Contingency = known risks, in or near baseline; Management = unknown-unknowns, outside baseline, management release
Monitor Reviews, risk audit, reserve analysis, technical performance analysis, owners assigned
Prompt lists PESTLE, TECOP, VUCA
Agile Risk-adjusted backlog; risk assessment each sprint; review each iteration; spikes [Beyond PMBOK 8]
Sustainability / security Register them with owners and active responses; transfer ≠ eliminate
Escalate Beyond scope/authority; receiving party must accept; team stops monitoring
Legacy terms [Beyond PMBOK 8] Residual risk, secondary risk, fallback plan, workaround
First-action pattern Check register/plan, assign owner, respond proportionately, use change control, keep it current
